name: Zane Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no links to AI firms, employers, unions or government, and this is confidential. What is your ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a service truck at Millstone mine, taking fuel and parts out to the loading machines. I joined three years ago after a warehouse closed, so I am still learning the mine roads at fifty-eight. I left school after secondary classes and have never used an AI tool. My partner and I have grown children, but we have less than a month’s expenses saved and retirement does not look close on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the drivers that if AI only changes a few forms, the service truck still needs fuel in it. I would keep the paper route sheet I know. Nobody gets a shovel moving on a tidy sentence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be relieved about the technology, but the mine already cancels a shift when a machine is down. My wages are low, and we have hardly any savings. There are not many other mine jobs near our town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep driving the service route and ask the foreman for any spare Saturday shift. In the first year I would put the extra pay toward the overdue heating bill if a shift came through. I would let the office clerk handle the new forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, even if the AI fuss fades. One missing Saturday shift hurts us more than a new computer story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if no Saturday shift came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call the heating company and ask for two payments. My partner has a little work at the market, but it changes week to week. I would not ask our son for rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the paper sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know which road floods after rain. The sheet has my pencil marks, and I do not trust a new screen to show them. I would learn it if the foreman made me, but I would not volunteer.

say: I would keep the **service truck** running while AI changes only a few office forms.
I would ask for **Saturday shifts** if the mine has any spare.
think: The **heating bill** and low wages already worry me despite little technological change.
Few **nearby mine jobs** leave me exposed to cancelled shifts.
do: **Keep** driving Millstone fuel and parts routes.
**Ask** the foreman for spare Saturday work and pay the heating bill if it comes.

steps.text: Keep driving Millstone fuel and parts routes
Ask heating company for two payments if Saturday work is unavailable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office can use AI for buying and scheduling, but somebody still has to bring fuel to a broken machine. I would ask the foreman to show us any new route sheet before changing shifts. I do not want the wrong parts sent to the wrong pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My truck work looks safer than an office desk for now, but a new schedule could squeeze junior drivers first. I only have three years here and there are few local openings. If hours dropped, our bills would be in trouble quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my route and write down every cancelled shift for a month. I would compare the new route sheet with my old one beside the foreman, even if it came on a screen. If I lost a full day, I would call the heating company before the bill went late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can manage a changed route with help, but I cannot absorb a lost day of pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake are you watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A parts delivery to the north pit when the loader is at the south pit. That can leave a crew waiting half a shift. My pencil sheet has the machine numbers beside the roads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you work at another mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but there are few nearby and I am a junior driver here. I would not leave a paying job just because a new screen annoyed me. I would look if the shifts actually went.

say: I would ask the foreman to show drivers the **new route sheet** before shifts change.
I would still deliver **fuel and parts** to broken machines.
think: My **junior shifts** could be cut even while service trucks remain hands-on.
A lost day of **pay** would put household bills behind quickly.
do: **Record** cancelled shifts and compare old and new routes beside the foreman.
**Call** the heating company before the bill falls overdue if a full day is lost.
feel: **Anxious** about lost hours despite confidence he can drive a changed route.
S1.quote: I can manage a changed route with help, but I cannot absorb a lost day of pay.
fieldNote: He sees **office tasks** changing first, but fears software may reduce junior driving shifts.
His response is **paper records** and a review with the foreman, rather than early AI learning.
He will seek a **payment plan** only if hours actually fall.

steps.text: Keep service route and record cancelled shifts for one month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the drivers full thinking AI by 2028 changes the office first, while capable service robots arrive around 2031. The mine might buy them and drop drivers. I would ask the foreman to tell us the purchase plan plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty when thinking AI arrives and sixty-three when capable robots appear. I would not have enough put aside to retire at sixty-three if this job went. My partner’s market pay is too small and uneven to carry both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel our plan to replace the old sofa this year and ask the pension office for a statement. I would keep driving after 2028 while people still run the service trucks. I would ask the foreman whether any parts-room jobs would remain, but I would not quit on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I would be awake working out how long one month’s money lasts when it is less than one month to begin with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the foreman has no purchase plan yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask again every few months and keep my paper route sheet. I cannot pay for a course with money we do not have. I would ask my partner to look at the pension letter with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They might bring groceries once, but each has a household of their own. I would not treat my children as a pension. I would ask about public help if the wage stopped.

say: I would ask for a **plain purchase plan** before capable service robots might arrive around 2031.
I would explain **2028** changes office thinking before hands-on trucks face robots.
think: At **sixty-three**, I could lose the service truck wage before I can afford retirement.
My partner’s **uneven market pay** cannot replace our main income.
do: **Request** a pension statement and review it with my partner.
**Keep** driving service trucks after 2028 while drivers remain.
feel: **Alarmed** by possible job loss before affordable retirement.
S2.quote: I would not treat my children as a pension.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **2028 office change** from capable robots around 2031.
Thin savings and uncertain **partner income** make job loss at sixty-three frightening.
He asks about parts-room jobs but does not assume a **transfer** exists.

steps.text: Cancel replacement of the old household sofa

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years before thinking AI and about eight before capable robots is enough time for the mine to be straight with us. I would ask the foreman for a written plan on driver posts. A family cannot make choices from rumours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-three in 2031 and about sixty-six in 2034 when robots become capable. I might reach retirement before the truck is replaced, but our savings are too small to count on that. If the mine cuts shifts early, even eight years does not help much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request my pension estimate this year and bring it home to my partner. I would keep driving and ask the parts manager for one supervised afternoon learning the storeroom, if there were real openings. If a paid storeroom training place appeared, I would take it while keeping my truck wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a little more room to breathe. I could learn a familiar parts job if somebody showed me slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the storeroom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already know many of the parts by sight. I would need help with the computer stock list, and I would not pretend otherwise. A paid storeroom place would let me learn without losing wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no place appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep driving and ask again the next quarter. I would not borrow for a training course at this age. The pension estimate would tell us whether waiting is possible.

say: I would ask for a **written driver plan** before capable robots might arrive around 2034.
I would keep **families informed** with dates instead of rumours.
think: At about **sixty-six** when robots become capable, retirement might still be unaffordable.
Early **shift cuts** could erase the value of extra warning.
do: **Request** a pension estimate this year and review it with my partner.
**Take** paid storeroom training if a real place appears while keeping truck wages.
**Keep** driving until a different paid post is actually offered.
feel: **Anxious**, but with time to try a familiar parts role.
S3.quote: A paid storeroom place would let me learn without losing wages.
fieldNote: He would be **sixty-three** at thinking AI and about sixty-six when robots become capable.
A **parts-room route** appeals because he knows parts, though he admits needing help with the stock computer.
Training is conditional on a **paid place** and continued truck wages.

steps.text: Take paid storeroom training if real place appears while retaining wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years to thinking AI and about thirteen to capable service robots gives the mine time to warn us properly. I would still ask for a written driver plan. The children are grown, but my partner and I need to know how we will pay our own bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-eight in 2036 and about seventy-one when robots become capable around 2039. I hope to be retired before then, but our savings today do not prove we can. The pension statement and steady shifts will decide more than the robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the service truck job while the mine offers shifts. I would request a pension statement this year and compare it with our heating and food bills. If the gap was large, I would ask a local advice worker what support or later work might be available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about retirement money, though the technology date itself is far away. I would feel better after seeing the actual numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you set a retirement date now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not without a statement and a budget. I would review both with my partner before giving up wages. Our children should not have to guess whether we can pay the heating bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful mine plan say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would say when service trucks might be replaced and which paid jobs remain for older drivers. I could live with a mine plan I disliked better than a blank page. I would show the plan to my partner.

say: I would ask for a **written driver plan** during the long warning.
I would keep taking **paid shifts** while checking whether retirement is affordable.
think: At about **seventy-one** when robots become capable, I hope to be retired but cannot assume it.
Today’s **thin savings** make the pension statement and steady shifts essential.
do: **Keep** driving service routes while paid shifts remain.
**Compare** pension statement with heating and food bills this year.
**Ask** a local advice worker about support if the pension gap is large.
feel: **Anxious** about retirement money despite the distant robot date.
S4.quote: I could live with a mine plan I disliked better than a blank page.
fieldNote: Capable robots at about **seventy-one** might arrive after retirement, which he cannot yet afford to assume.
He wants **plain figures** and a written driver plan rather than a new tool.
His **existing bill pressure** remains even with thirteen years before capable robots.

steps.text: Keep driving Millstone service routes while paid shifts remain

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable service robots could arrive around 2031, before I can afford to retire. A written plan for driver posts and a paid route into parts work would help. I would need the pension estimate too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to people who started at the mine late because other work closed. Three years here has not built a retirement fund. I can learn a parts list if someone shows me, but I cannot make wages appear from a screen.

headlineQuote: I can learn a parts list if someone shows me, but I cannot make wages appear from a screen.
portrait: Zane Schmidt is a **58-year-old** junior service truck driver at Millstone mine who entered after a warehouse closure.
He and his partner have grown children, **low pay**, irregular market income and less than a month of expenses saved.
He trusts a **paper route sheet** and avoids AI tools, but would learn a paid storeroom role with patient supervision.
Even mild change leaves him **anxious** about bills; faster robot availability threatens wages before affordable retirement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because capable service robots could arrive around 2031 before retirement is affordable.
whatWouldHelp: A **written driver plan**, paid route into parts work and pension estimate would help him plan around a possible lost wage.
